topics.intro: This topic tells the story of computing, from the abacus and the early calculating machines to the five generations of computers. You will learn who invented what, and what technology marks each generation.

sections.title: Early calculating devices
body: Long before electricity, people built tools to help them count and calculate. Learning them in order tells the story of computing.

**The abacus** is a frame with beads on rods. It is thousands of years old, and it is still used in some countries. A skilled abacus operator can add and subtract at the speed of a **person using a hand calculator.**

**John Napier** (Scotland, early 1600s) invented **logarithms**, which turn multiplication into addition. He also made **Napier's bones**, rods used for multiplication. The **slide rule** was built soon after, using logarithms.

**Blaise Pascal** (France, 1642) built the **Pascaline**, the first mechanical calculator. It added and subtracted using gears. **Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** (Germany, 1670s) built the **Stepped Reckoner**, a four-function calculator: it could add, subtract, multiply and divide.
**Joseph-Marie Jacquard** (France, 1801) used **punched cards** to control a weaving loom. Punched cards later became the way to feed programs and data into computers.

**Charles Babbage** (England, 1800s), often called the father of the computer, designed two machines. The **Difference Engine** (a steam-driven calculating machine for tables) and the **Analytical Engine**, which had the same main parts as a modern computer: input, a store, a processing 'mill' and output. **Ada Lovelace** wrote notes on it that are considered the first computer program.
**Herman Hollerith** (USA, 1890) built a punched-card machine for the census, and his company later became part of IBM.
**ENIAC** did not exist before the 19th century. It was built in the 1940s, so it is the odd one out among the old devices.
keyPoints: Napier: logarithms and Napier's bones. Pascal: Pascaline (first mechanical calculator). Leibniz: Stepped Reckoner.
Babbage: Difference Engine and Analytical Engine.

example.answer: Pascal: Pascaline. Leibniz: Stepped Reckoner. Babbage: Difference and Analytical Engines

sections.title: The five generations of computers
body: Computers are grouped into **generations**, based on the main technology inside them. The first machine often called the forefather of today's all-electronic digital computers is **ENIAC** (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, 1940s). EDVAC and UNIVAC followed, and **UNIVAC I** was the first commercial computer.
**First generation (1940s to mid-1950s): vacuum tubes.** Machines were huge, hot and used machine language. Input was by punched cards and tapes, and magnetic drums were used for memory.

**Second generation (late 1950s to 1960s): transistors** replaced vacuum tubes. Computers became smaller, faster and cheaper. Assembly languages and early high-level languages such as **FORTRAN** and **COBOL** appeared. Input was still mostly **punched cards**. **Grace Hopper** created **FLOW-MATIC**, an early English-like language that led to COBOL.

**Third generation (1960s to 1970s): integrated circuits (ICs)**, many transistors on one small chip. Keyboards and monitors replaced punched cards, and operating systems let several programs run together.
**Fourth generation (1970s onwards): microprocessors**, a whole CPU on one chip. This brought **personal computers** and **graphical user interfaces (GUIs)**, with icons, windows and a mouse.
**Fifth generation (now and future): artificial intelligence.** The goals include computers that understand **natural (human) language**, learn and reason, and use parallel processing.

**Classes of computers by size:** supercomputers (fastest, speed measured in **FLOPS**, floating point operations per second), mainframes (large organisations), minicomputers, and **microcomputers** (desktop, laptop, notebook). EDVAC is an early machine, **not** a microcomputer.
keyPoints: 1st vacuum tubes; 2nd transistors; 3rd integrated circuits; 4th microprocessors and GUIs; 5th artificial intelligence.
Second generation used punched cards for input.

topics.intro: Computers store everything in binary. This topic covers bits, bytes, words, the number of values n bits can hold, character codes, and converting numbers between decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.

sections.title: Bits, bytes and storage units
body: A computer stores everything as **0s and 1s.** One binary digit is a **bit.** Bits are grouped to make bigger units.

**4 bits = 1 nibble.** A nibble is enough to hold one **hexadecimal** digit or one **BCD** digit. **8 bits = 1 byte**, the **smallest addressable** unit of memory, and enough for one character. A **word** is the group of bits a computer handles at once: a 32-bit word has 32 ÷ 8 = **4 bytes** (and 8 nibbles).
**Counting values.** With n bits you can make **2ⁿ** different values. 8 bits give 2⁸ = 256. 16 bits give 2¹⁶ = **65,536.** Each extra bit doubles the number.

**Big units:** 1 kilobyte (KB) is about a thousand bytes (exactly 1024), 1 megabyte (MB) is about a million, 1 gigabyte (GB) is about a **billion** bytes, and 1 terabyte (TB) is about a trillion. So 5 GB is roughly **five billion** bytes.

**Character codes.** Letters, digits and symbols are stored as numbers. **ASCII** uses 7 bits, so it has **128** characters. **Extended ASCII** uses 8 bits and has **256** characters. **Unicode** is bigger and covers the world's languages.
**BCD (Binary Coded Decimal)** writes each decimal digit using **4 bits.** The number 259 is 0010 0101 1001 in BCD (2, 5 and 9 each in four bits).
keyPoints: 4 bits = nibble. 8 bits = byte. A 32-bit word = 4 bytes.
ASCII 128, extended ASCII 256. BCD uses 4 bits per digit.

sections.title: Converting between binary and decimal
body: A number system is described by its **base.** Decimal is base 10 (digits 0-9). Binary is base 2 (digits 0 and 1). Octal is base 8 (0-7). Hexadecimal is base 16 (0-9 and A-F, where A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15).
**Binary to decimal.** Write the place values from the right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128… Add the place values where the digit is 1. For **1100111₂:** 64 + 32 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 1 = **103.**
**Fractions in binary.** After the point the places are ½, ¼, ⅛… For **11011.101₂:** the whole part 11011 = 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 27. The fraction .101 = ½ + ⅛ = 0.625. So the answer is **27.625.**

**Decimal to binary (whole numbers).** Divide by 2 again and again, and write the remainders from bottom to top. Example 45: 45 ÷ 2 = 22 r 1, 22 ÷ 2 = 11 r 0, 11 ÷ 2 = 5 r 1, 5 ÷ 2 = 2 r 1, 2 ÷ 2 = 1 r 0, 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Reading upwards: **101101₂.**

**Decimal fractions to binary.** Multiply the fraction by 2 again and again, and take the whole-number part each time. 15.15: 15 = 1111₂. For 0.15: 0.15 × 2 = 0.3 (0), 0.6 (0), 1.2 (1), 0.4 (0), 0.8 (0), 1.6 (1), 1.2 (1), 0.4 (0)… so 0.15 = 0.00100110…₂ and it never ends. So 15.15 is **1111.00100110…₂**. A question that offers 1111.11 or 1111.01 is wrong. Hint: the fraction .15 is less than ¼, so the first two binary places are 0.
**512 in binary** is 2⁹, so a 1 followed by nine 0s: **1000000000₂.** Powers of 2 are always a 1 followed by zeros.
keyPoints: Whole numbers to binary: divide by 2, read remainders upwards.
Fractions to binary: multiply by 2, take the whole parts.

sections.title: Octal and hexadecimal
body: Octal and hex are shortcuts for writing long binary numbers. **One octal digit = 3 binary bits. One hex digit = 4 binary bits.**
**Binary to octal:** group the bits in threes **from the point outwards** (add zeros if needed). **11100101₂:** 011 100 101 = 3, 4, 5. So **345₈.**
**Hex to binary:** replace each hex digit with its 4 bits. **12₁₆:** 1 = 0001, 2 = 0010, so 00010010 = **10010₂.**

**Hex to octal:** go through binary. **A45₁₆:** A = 1010, 4 = 0100, 5 = 0101, giving 101001000101. Regroup in threes: 101 001 000 101 = 5, 1, 0, 5. So **5105₈.** (An option list like 5739, 5379 or 3957 would not contain this answer.)
keyPoints: Octal digit = 3 bits. Hex digit = 4 bits.
Group from the point outwards; pad with zeros.

topics.intro: This topic covers the physical parts of a computer: the system unit and peripherals, the CPU and its machine cycle, and the different kinds of memory and storage.

sections.title: Hardware: system unit and peripherals
body: **Hardware** is every physical part of a computer that you can touch. It is classified into two groups: the **system unit** and the **peripherals**.

The **system unit** is the box that holds the motherboard, the **CPU**, memory, the power supply and the drives. **Peripherals** are the devices connected to it: input devices (keyboard, mouse), output devices (monitor, printer) and storage devices.

**Pointing and drawing devices.** A **stylus** looks like a ballpoint pen but uses pressure, not ink, to write text and draw lines on a pad or screen. A **light pen** is pointed at the screen. A **trackball** is like an upside-down mouse: you roll the ball with your thumb. A **joystick** is a lever used mostly for games.
**Hardcopy and softcopy.** Output on paper, such as a **printout**, is **hardcopy.** Output on a screen is **softcopy.**
**Data and information.** **Data** is raw facts and figures. **Information** is data that has been processed so that it is useful.

**Network hardware** lets computers talk to each other: **modem, router, hub, switch, repeater, bridge and gateway.** A **repeater** boosts a weak signal so it can travel further. **Bandwidth** is the data transfer capacity of a connection.
**Auxiliary devices** are extra devices, such as a UPS, a scanner or an external drive. A **bridge** is a network device, not an auxiliary device.
keyPoints: Network devices: modem, router, hub, repeater, bridge, gateway.

sections.title: The CPU and the machine cycle
body: The **central processing unit (CPU)** is the brain of the computer. It has three main parts.

The **control unit** reads program instructions one after another (**sequential** interpretation and execution) and directs the other parts. The **arithmetic and logic unit (ALU)** does arithmetic (+, −, ×, ÷) and logical comparisons, so it resolves expressions such as x − y = x + 1. **Registers** are tiny, very fast storage places inside the CPU.

**The machine cycle** is the set of steps the CPU repeats for every instruction: **fetch** (get the instruction from memory), **decode** (work out what it means), **execute** (carry it out) and **store** (write the result). **Coding** is something a programmer does, so it is **not** part of the machine cycle.
**Speed.** CPU speed is measured by the **clock speed** in hertz: megahertz (MHz) or gigahertz (GHz). A higher clock speed means more cycles per second.
keyPoints: Machine cycle: fetch, decode, execute, store.
Coding is not part of the machine cycle.

sections.title: Memory and storage
body: **Primary memory** is directly used by the CPU. **Secondary storage** keeps data permanently (hard disk, flash drive, DVD).

**RAM (random access memory)** lets any location be reached in a fixed, short time after its address is given. It is **volatile**: when power goes off, the contents are lost. **DRAM** (dynamic) needs refreshing and is cheaper. **SRAM** (static) is faster and is used for cache.

**ROM (read-only memory)** is **non-volatile** and holds start-up instructions. The family: **ROM** (fixed at the factory), **PROM** (programmable once), **EPROM** (erasable with ultraviolet light and reprogrammable) and **EEPROM** (erased electrically).
**Storage capacity** is how much a disk can hold. Common units are KB, MB, GB and TB.

topics.intro: This topic explains software types, what the operating system does, how a computer boots, and how programs are translated, linked and loaded.

sections.title: What software is and its types
body: **Software** is a set of instructions that directs a computer to perform a task. A single set of such instructions is called a **program.**
**System software** controls and runs the computer. Examples: operating systems, translators, utilities. **Application software** does a user's task: word processing, spreadsheets, games.
**Examples of operating systems:** Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, Unix. **HP** is a computer manufacturer, not an operating system.
**Office suites** bundle applications. In Microsoft Office, **Outlook** supports communication and email, Word is for documents, Excel for spreadsheets and PowerPoint for presentations.
keyPoints: System software runs the computer; application software serves the user.

steps: Windows runs the computer: system software.

sections.title: The operating system and booting
body: The **operating system (OS)** manages hardware and software resources. Its jobs include managing memory, files, processes and devices, and giving the user an interface.
The OS has two kinds of parts. The **control program** (also called the **master program**, containing the **kernel**) supervises everything. **Service programs** do extra jobs.

**Booting** is starting a computer. A **cold boot** is switching on a computer that is off. A **warm boot** is restarting a computer that is already on (for example Ctrl+Alt+Del). It is **not** true that a warm boot is turning on a computer after it has been shut down.
At start-up the **POST** (power-on self-test) checks the hardware, then the **BIOS** in ROM loads the operating system.
**Virtual machine** operating systems **do** let a single user run two or more operating systems at the same time.
keyPoints: Cold boot = from off; warm boot = restart.
POST then BIOS (in ROM) then OS.

sections.title: Translators, utilities and language generations
body: A computer only understands **machine language.** **Translators** convert programs into it: an **assembler** (assembly language), a **compiler** (whole program at once) and an **interpreter** (line by line).

A **linker** brings together object modules, operating system routines and other utility software to produce an **executable program.** The **loader** places it in memory. **Linking and loading** are done by system programs. Linking and loading are system-software jobs that prepare a program to run.
**Utility programs** do housekeeping jobs: backup, disk clean-up, virus scan, file compression.

**Generations of languages.** 1GL machine language; 2GL assembly language; 3GL high-level languages such as C and Java; **4GL** are **non-procedural and problem-oriented** (SQL, report generators). So the statement '4GLs are not problem-oriented' is **false.**
**Gopher** is an older menu-based document-retrieval protocol. The protocol governing the transfer of hypertext is **HTTP**, not Gopher.

topics.intro: This topic covers how the Internet began, the protocols and services it provides, and the words you must know: ISP, modem, browser, host, URL and caching.

sections.title: What the Internet is and how it began
body: The **Internet** is a worldwide network of computers. It began with **ARPANET**, the first network that planted the seed of the Internet (funded by the US Department of Defense, late 1960s).

Computers talk through **protocols**, agreed rules. **TCP/IP** is the foundational protocol suite of the Internet. Every device has an **IP address**, and IP addresses are **unique**. A **domain name** (for example example.com) is an easy name for an IP address.

A **server** on the Internet is also called a **host.** A **browser** is the application software that lets you view information on the **World Wide Web (WWW)**. The first page you normally see at a website is its **home page.**
To connect a home to the Internet you need a **modem** and an **Internet Service Provider (ISP)**, the company that gives you access.
**Caching** keeps frequently accessed pages or addresses in memory for future use, which makes loading faster.
**WAP (Wireless Application Protocol)** was used for Internet access on early mobile phones.
keyPoints: ARPANET began it; TCP/IP is the protocol suite.
Server = host; browser views the Web.

sections.title: Protocols, URLs and services
body: **HTTP** transfers web pages (hypertext) and is the protocol for the WWW. **FTP** transfers files between computers, so users get files from the Internet using FTP. **SMTP** sends email. **Telnet** is for remote login.

A **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) is a web address, for example https://www.example.com/page.html. It has a protocol, a domain name and a path. A URL is not made of letters and numbers only: it also contains symbols such as : / and .
**Services of the Internet:** email, web browsing, file transfer, online chat and video calls, e-commerce. **Word processing** is not an Internet service; it is application software.
**Email** is fast, but **viruses can spread through email attachments**, so the statement 'viruses cannot be spread via email' is false.
**Distance learning (e-learning)** is education where the tutor and the learner are geographically apart.
**Benefits of the Internet:** easy access to information, and online marketing and e-commerce opportunities for businesses.
keyPoints: HTTP web, FTP files, SMTP email.

topics.intro: This topic shows where computers are used, from healthcare to manufacturing, and covers computer ethics, intellectual property and plagiarism.

sections.title: Computer applications in different fields
body: Computers are used in almost every field.

**Healthcare:** diagnosing diseases and keeping patient records. **Education:** online learning and virtual classrooms; ICT makes teaching and learning more effective. **Law:** legal research and managing case files. **Transportation:** **GPS** (global positioning system) for navigation.
**Manufacturing:** **CAD** (computer-aided design) helps design products; **CAM** (computer-aided manufacturing) controls machines, such as robots assembling cars.

**Simulation** uses software and hardware to create an artificial model of a real situation, for training or testing. **Virtual reality (VR)** gives a 3D experience; architects use it to show clients a 3D preview of a building and landscape.
**Command and control systems** (such as air-traffic control or defence) must be designed as **fault-tolerant systems**, which keep working even if a part fails.
A **barcode** is a product identification code made of vertical lines and spaces, read by a scanner. **Edutainment** simplifies learning through songs and animations.

sections.title: Ethics, intellectual property and plagiarism
body: **Ethics** is the set of principles and moral standards for using computers. **Ethical standards** promote trust, good behaviour and fairness, and govern conduct.
The **Ten Commandments of Computer Ethics** were created by the **Computer Ethics Institute.**

**Intellectual property rights** are entitlements of persons for the creativity of their minds. Legal protection of an invention takes these forms: **patents, trade secrets, trademarks and copyrights.** 'Trade Rights' is not one of them.
Owning a **patent** means others must seek and receive the owner's permission to use the technology.
**Plagiarism** is copying and publishing someone else's work without proper citation. **Open source software** has few or no copyright restrictions: users can see and change its code.
**Social effects** of computers can be a double-edged sword: online social networks connect people but can also foster misinformation, a problem of information veracity and control.
keyPoints: Forms of protection: patent, trade secret, trademark, copyright.

steps: Using another's work as your own, without credit.

sections.title: The program development cycle and algorithms
body: **Analysis, design, coding and execution** are stages of the **program development cycle.** The usual stages: problem definition and analysis, design (algorithm, flowchart, pseudocode), coding, testing and debugging, documentation and maintenance.
**Problem definition and analysis** is critical, because an incomplete understanding here produces a program that correctly solves the wrong problem.

An **algorithm** is a step-by-step solution to a problem. To develop one, you understand the problem, plan the steps and check them. **Coding the plan** is a later stage, so it is not a step in developing the algorithm itself.
A good program has qualities such as correctness, efficiency and **maintainability**, which makes it easy for others to understand and modify.
keyPoints: Cycle: analyse, design, code, test, document.
Poor analysis gives a program solving the wrong problem.

example.problem: Why spend time on analysis before coding?
steps: Mistakes in understanding carry through every later stage.
The result may work but solve the wrong problem.

sections.title: Flowcharts, pseudocode and control structures
body: A **flowchart** is a diagram of the steps of a solution, with symbols joined by arrows. Advantages: it gives a **visual representation** of the logic, which aids understanding. Limitation: for complex systems it can become **cumbersome and difficult** to draw and change. A flowchart is **not** ambiguous; it must be clear.
**Guideline:** each processing symbol should have **only one entry point and exactly one exit point.**
**Pseudocode** is the algorithm written in plain, code-like English. Its correct order is: **header, declaration, body, termination.**

**Control structures** decide the order of execution. **Sequence** runs steps in order. **Selection** chooses a path: IF-THEN-ELSE, and the CASE (switch-case) statement, which is a specialised selection. **Repetition (iteration)** repeats steps: WHILE and FOR loops.
Example of repetition: summing 1 to 5 with a loop. total = 0; for i in 1..5: total = total + i. Result 15.
keyPoints: Flowchart: visual, one entry/one exit per process symbol, can be cumbersome when large.
Pseudocode order: header, declaration, body, termination.

example.problem: Trace: total = 0; for i = 1 to 5: total = total + i. Find total.

sections.title: Types of programming errors
body: There are three types of errors.

**Syntax error:** a rule of the language is broken, for example a **missing semicolon or curly bracket**, or using a **keyword or reserved word as a variable name.** The compiler detects it, so it is found during compilation. **Data mismatch** is not a syntax error.

**Runtime error:** the program is correct to the compiler, but it fails when it runs because it attempts an operation that is syntactically valid but impossible. Example: finding the square root of a negative number in real arithmetic, or dividing by zero.

**Logical error:** the program runs and gives an **incorrect result** because the logic is wrong. Example: entering a wrong salary scale in payroll. Logical errors are the **most difficult to detect**, because no error message appears.
So 'missing curly brackets and semicolons are runtime errors' is false: they are syntax errors.
keyPoints: Syntax: grammar rules; found at compilation.
Runtime: fails while running (sqrt of negative).
Logical: wrong results, hardest to detect.

example.problem: Classify: (a) missing semicolon, (b) square root of -4, (c) wrong tax rate.
